vocab.articleQuote: The author is a self-important dilettante.
vocab.inContext: Graham uses this imaginary insult as an example of dressed-up name-calling: the commenter dismisses the writer as a dabbler with no real expertise instead of engaging with anything the writer actually argued.
vocab.meaning: A person who dabbles in a subject casually, for fun or for show, without serious study or commitment.
examples: After one week of guitar practice he was calling himself a musician, but his teacher gently hinted he was still a dilettante.
She quit three clubs in two months, and her brother teased her for being a dilettante who never stuck with anything.

vocab.articleQuote: I can't believe the author dismisses intelligent design in such a cavalier fashion.
vocab.inContext: The imaginary commenter is complaining about the author's attitude — brushing off an idea casually, without giving it what the commenter considers serious, respectful attention.
vocab.meaning: Showing a careless, offhand lack of concern about something other people take seriously.
examples: He was so cavalier about the final exam that he didn't even open the study guide.
Her cavalier attitude toward the group project frustrated the teammates who had worked all weekend on it.

vocab.articleQuote: An eloquent speaker or writer can give the impression of vanquishing an opponent merely by using forceful words. In fact that is probably the defining quality of a demagogue.
vocab.inContext: Graham says that winning an argument through sheer force of words — sounding powerful rather than being right — is the signature move of a demagogue.
vocab.meaning: A leader or speaker who wins people over by stirring up their emotions and prejudices instead of offering honest arguments.
examples: The candidate for class president sounded like a demagogue, shouting crowd-pleasing promises about banning homework instead of explaining a real plan.
History classes study how demagogues in the 1930s used fear and anger, not facts, to take power.

vocab.articleQuote: Is the author flippant, but correct? Better that than grave and wrong.
vocab.inContext: Graham asks whether a writer with a joking, unserious tone can still be right — and answers yes: a flippant-but-correct writer beats a solemn-but-wrong one, which is why criticizing tone alone is weak.
vocab.meaning: Treating something serious with casual humor or a lack of proper respect.
examples: His flippant answer — "homework is a myth" — got a laugh from the class and a frown from the teacher.
She regretted her flippant reply when she realized her friend was genuinely upset.

concepts.name: Ad hominem
concepts.articleQuote: An ad hominem attack is not quite as weak as mere name-calling. It might actually carry some weight.
concepts.meaning:
In soccer there's a foul called "playing the player, not the ball" — you can't tackle the person just because you can't get the ball. An ad hominem (Latin for "to the person") is the arguing version of that foul: instead of showing what's wrong with someone's argument, you attack the someone.

Graham's example: a senator writes that senators' salaries should be raised, and a critic answers, "Of course he would say that. He's a senator." Notice what happened — the critic pointed at the senator's motive, but never showed the argument was wrong. Maybe salaries really should be raised! The senator's self-interest is a reason to double-check his logic, not a substitute for checking it. As Graham puts it: if something is wrong with the argument, say what it is; if nothing is, the arguer's identity doesn't matter.

A common version is attacking someone's authority instead of their claim: "You can't have an opinion on the team's strategy — you don't even play." But good ideas often come from outsiders, and a true statement is true no matter who says it. Once you know the name, you'll spot ad hominems everywhere: in comment sections, in politics, and in arguments with your siblings.

concepts.name: Straw man
concepts.articleQuote: If you can't find an actual quote to disagree with, you may be arguing with a straw man.
concepts.meaning:
A scarecrow is much easier to knock over than a real person — it's made of straw and it can't fight back. A straw man argument is when you build a fake, exaggerated version of what someone said, knock *that* over, and act like you won.

Here's how it works. Your friend says, "I think we get a bit too much homework." You reply, "Oh, so school should just teach us nothing at all?" You've now defeated an argument — but not your friend's argument. Nobody said school should teach nothing. You invented a weaker claim (a scarecrow), stuffed it, and beat it up, because the real claim was harder to answer.

Graham gives a practical test for catching yourself doing this: to genuinely refute someone, you should be able to quote the exact words you disagree with. If you can't find a real quote that says what you're attacking, you may be arguing with a straw man you built yourself. Keep that test handy when you read online arguments — you'll be surprised how often the comment is fighting something the article never actually said.

quiz.question: According to Graham, what is the most convincing form of disagreement?
options: Pointing out that the author lacks authority on the topic
Refuting the author's central point, with a quote and reasons it's mistaken
Stating the opposing position clearly and confidently
Correcting the author's grammar and minor factual slips
quiz.explanation: The top of the hierarchy (DH6) is refuting the central point — quoting the key claim and explaining why it's wrong; everything below it proves less.

quiz.question: A commenter writes: "Of course she supports longer lunch periods — she runs the cafeteria." Which form of disagreement is this?
options: A straw man
A refutation
An ad hominem
A counterargument
quiz.explanation: It attacks the arguer's motive and position instead of showing anything wrong with the argument itself — the definition of ad hominem.

quiz.question: Someone proposes one mental-health day per semester, and a classmate replies: "So you think students should just skip school whenever they feel like it?" What has the classmate done?
options: Refuted the central point
Attacked a straw man — an exaggerated claim nobody made
Responded to the proposer's tone
Made a valid counterargument with evidence
quiz.explanation: The reply defeats an invented, extreme version of the proposal ("skip whenever you feel like it") rather than the modest claim actually made — a classic straw man.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses the word "cavalier" correctly?
options: The cavalier was parked in the driveway overnight.
He cavaliered the ball across the field to his teammate.
The chef added a cavalier of spices to the soup.
She gave a cavalier shrug when told the test counted for half her grade.
quiz.explanation: Cavalier is an adjective meaning carelessly unconcerned about something serious — shrugging off a huge test fits exactly.

quiz.question: Why does Graham say the disagreement hierarchy can't be used to pick the winner of an argument?
options: Because the levels describe the form of a reply, not whether it's actually correct
Because most online arguments never rise above name-calling
Because refutation is too rare for anyone to achieve
Because lower levels are often more persuasive to readers
quiz.explanation: A reply at the top level (DH6) can still be mistaken — the hierarchy sets an upper bound on how convincing a reply can be, but form alone doesn't make it true.
